title: Is the very brief run-time of movies a prime reason why far more films get translated more than any other medium (esp TV shows) except maybe books?

commenti.body:
If I understand correctly, you are asking why there are more foreign films with English subtitles (or dubs) available than there are foreign television shows with English subtitles (or dubs).  For the most part, it really does not have to do with the runtime.  It's that films have been internationally spread for decades, whereas television shows are only now starting to get this treatment.

Consider the difference in how films and TV shows were distributed prior to the advent of streaming only 10-15 years ago.  Films were originally distributed to theaters, both chain theaters and independent theaters.  Independent theater owners in the English speaking world have never been shy about allowing foreign films to play in their theaters, which created many subtitled foreign films as early as the 1920's.  The Oscars introduced a foreign film category in the 1950's further accelerating the rate in which foreign films were distributed to English speakers.  Once home video debuted, more foreign films were able to be distributed and more translation work was needed.  Home video started with the VHS, which had just about enough room for 1 film.

Now contrast this with television.  Television, up until about 10 years ago, was widely considered to be the lesser medium.  People dreamt of being movies stars, not TV stars.  Before streaming, television shows could only distributed one way: from a network to the television set.  Networks are very regional and rarely license television shows from foreign countries.  Thus, there was never a need to translate these shows.  And, there wasn't a home video market for television shows until the introduction of the DVD in the early 2000s, and even then, film was more prominent there.

Problem with your conclusion is that it ignores the rest of the world practically all A listers come from TV first before movie and TV was actually the next stage in an actor's careers after making a name in theater as seen in the UK. And despite making it big not just in their country but even in Hollywood, a lot of foreign stars still continued in acting on TV programs and not just high budget miniseries but even network stuff such as soap operas and brainless no-continuity action shows.

Practically all James Bonds except Connery and Lazenby were in TV before becoming Bond and more or less continued doinga  mix of TV, theater, and film (including Connery later on in his career). And that proves how wrong your assumption is.

My relatives in-laws are from India and movie stars coming from TV background is normal and same with A listers doing TV programs. And it has been this way as far as the 70s, even roles already casting top names asearly as the 50s.

Prestige TV was already nothing new in Europe with Poland producing Dekalog, the BBC having a hosts of nonstop release of high quality shows with the best actors from theater in the UK, and pretty much ore or less the major networks of Germany, France, and Italy (the top media powerhouses of Europe in the past and even today) still producing miniseries with actors who perform at Shakespearan level and arguably superior to even a a lot of non-Oscar winning A listers in America. The USSR's programs were in the same bot even though Russia lags behind today.

So no, your overall conclusion is pretty off the mark in the history of both mediums esp in the rest of the world. Even countries with horrible TV today like Japan and China have a long history of producing high budget miniseries that can match with Oscar nominees in at least acting and writing (even if stuff like art set and costumes lag behind due to obvious budget reasons).

I feel like you are primarily taking issue with my statement that TV was seen as the lesser medium. But, a couple of things: First, that statement has no effect on everything else I said.

And second, that sentiment absolutely existed in America.  It does not matter if the rest of the world treated TV as equal to film.  Americans treated TV as lesser, so there was less incentive to import foreign TV shows and thus they did not need to be translated for that audience.
